displayName: Letter 6.16 (to Tacitus, on the death of Pliny the Elder)

sentences.latin: Petis ut tibi avunculi mei exitum scribam, quo verius tradere posteris possis.
sentences.english: You ask that I write to you about the death of my uncle, so that you may be able to hand it down to posterity more truthfully.

sentences.latin: Gratias ago; nam video morti eius si celebretur a te immortalem gloriam esse propositam.
sentences.english: I thank you; for I see that, if his death is celebrated by you, an immortal glory has been set forth for it.

sentences.latin: Quamvis enim pulcherrimarum clade terrarum, ut populi ut urbes memorabili casu, quasi semper victurus occiderit, quamvis ipse plurima opera et mansura condiderit, multum tamen perpetuitati eius scriptorum tuorum aeternitas addet.
sentences.english: For although he perished in the destruction of the most beautiful of lands, like peoples, like cities perish in memorable disaster, as if destined to live forever, and although he himself founded many enduring works, nevertheless the eternity of your writings will add much to his perpetuity.

sentences.latin: Equidem beatos puto, quibus deorum munere datum est aut facere scribenda aut scribere legenda, beatissimos vero quibus utrumque.
sentences.english: I consider those blessed, indeed, to whom it has been given by the gift of the gods either to do things worth writing about or to write things worth reading, but those most blessed to whom both have been given.

sentences.latin: Horum in numero avunculus meus et suis libris et tuis erit.
sentences.english: Among the number of these my uncle will be, both through his own books and through yours.

sentences.latin: Quo libentius suscipio, deposco etiam quod iniungis.
sentences.english: And so I undertake the more willingly, I even demand, what you enjoin.

sentences.latin: Erat Miseni classemque imperio praesens regebat.
sentences.english: He was at Misenum and was commanding the fleet in person with full authority.

sentences.latin: Nonum kal. Septembres hora fere septima mater mea indicat ei apparere nubem inusitata et magnitudine et specie.
sentences.english: On the ninth day before the Kalends of September, around the seventh hour, my mother points out to him that a cloud is appearing, unusual in both size and shape.

sentences.latin: Usus ille sole, mox frigida, gustaverat iacens studebatque; poscit soleas, ascendit locum ex quo maxime miraculum illud conspici poterat.
sentences.english: He, having taken the sun, then a cold bath, had eaten lying down and was studying; he asks for his sandals and climbs to a place from which that marvel could best be observed.

sentences.latin: Nubes — incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte (Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est) — oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit.
sentences.english: A cloud was rising — it was unclear to those watching from afar from which mountain (it was later known to have been Vesuvius) — and no tree could more closely express its likeness and shape than the pine.

sentences.latin: Nam longissimo velut trunco elata in altum quibusdam ramis diffundebatur, credo quia recenti spiritu evecta, dein senescente eo destituta aut etiam pondere suo victa in latitudinem vanescebat, candida interdum, interdum sordida et maculosa prout terram cineremve sustulerat.
sentences.english: For lifted up to a great height as if on a very long trunk, it spread out into branches, I suppose because it was carried up by a fresh blast, then, as that blast weakened, the cloud was left unsupported, or even overcome by its own weight, and was dispersing laterally, sometimes white, sometimes dirty and spotted, depending on whether it had carried up earth or ash.

sentences.latin: Magnum propiusque noscendum ut eruditissimo viro visum.
sentences.english: It seemed to him, as a most learned man, a great matter and one to be examined more closely.

sentences.latin: Iubet liburnicam aptari; mihi si venire una vellem facit copiam; respondi studere me malle, et forte ipse quod scriberem dederat.
sentences.english: He orders a swift boat to be made ready; he gives me the opportunity to come along if I wish; I replied that I preferred to study, and by chance he himself had given me something to write.

sentences.latin: Egrediebatur domo; accipit codicillos Rectinae Tasci imminenti periculo exterritae (nam villa eius subiacebat, nec ulla nisi navibus fuga): ut se tanto discrimini eriperet orabat.
sentences.english: He was going out of the house; he receives a note from Rectina, the wife of Tascus, terrified by the imminent danger (for her villa lay below the mountain, and there was no escape except by ship): she begged that he rescue her from such great peril.

sentences.latin: Vertit ille consilium et quod studioso animo incohaverat obit maximo.
sentences.english: He changed his plan, and what he had begun in a scholarly spirit he carried out in the greatest one.

sentences.latin: Deducit quadriremes, ascendit ipse non Rectinae modo sed multis (erat enim frequens amoenitas orae) laturus auxilium.
sentences.english: He launches the quadriremes and embarks himself, intending to bring help not only to Rectina but to many (for the pleasantness of the coast was popular).

sentences.latin: Properat illuc unde alii fugiunt, rectumque cursum recta gubernacula in periculum tenet adeo solutus metu, ut omnes illius mali motus omnes figuras ut deprenderat oculis dictaret enotaretque.
sentences.english: He hurries to the place from which others are fleeing, and holds a straight course and straight rudders into the danger, so free from fear that he was dictating and noting down every motion, every shape of that disaster as he had grasped them with his eyes.

sentences.latin: Iam navibus cinis incidebat, quo propius accederent, calidior et densior; iam pumices etiam nigrique et ambusti et fracti igne lapides; iam vadum subitum ruinaque montis litora obstantia.
sentences.english: Already ash was falling on the ships, the closer they approached, the hotter and denser; already pumice stones too and stones blackened and burned and shattered by fire; already a sudden shallow and shores blocked by the collapse of the mountain.

sentences.latin: Cunctatus paulum an retro flecteret, mox gubernatori ut ita faceret monenti 'Fortes' inquit 'fortuna iuvat: Pomponianum pete.'
sentences.english: Having hesitated a little whether to turn back, then, when the helmsman was advising him to do so, he said, 'Fortune favors the brave: make for Pomponianus.'

sentences.latin: Stabiis erat diremptus sinu medio (nam sensim circumactis curvatisque litoribus mare infunditur); ibi quamquam nondum periculo appropinquante, conspicuo tamen et cum cresceret proximo, sarcinas contulerat in naves, certus fugae si contrarius ventus resedisset.
sentences.english: He was at Stabiae, separated by the middle of the bay (for the sea pours in along shores that gradually curve and bend); there, although the danger was not yet near, but in plain sight and, as it grew, very close, he had loaded his belongings onto ships, resolved on flight if the contrary wind should die down.

sentences.latin: Quo tunc avunculus meus secundissimo invectus, complectitur trepidantem consolatur hortatur, utque timorem eius sua securitate leniret, deferri in balineum iubet; lotus accubat cenat, aut hilaris aut (quod aeque magnum) similis hilari.
sentences.english: Carried in by this most favorable wind, my uncle then embraces him as he trembles, consoles him, encourages him, and so that he might soothe his fear by his own calm, orders himself to be carried into the bath; bathed, he reclines and dines, either cheerful or (which is equally great) seeming cheerful.

sentences.latin: Interim e Vesuvio monte pluribus locis latissimae flammae altaque incendia relucebant, quorum fulgor et claritas tenebris noctis excitabatur.
sentences.english: Meanwhile, from Mount Vesuvius in several places very wide flames and tall fires were shining out, whose brightness and clarity was made greater by the darkness of the night.

sentences.latin: Ille agrestium trepidatione ignes relictos desertasque villas per solitudinem ardere in remedium formidinis dictitabat.
sentences.english: He, to remedy their fear, kept saying that the fires were left behind by the panic of the country folk and that the abandoned villas were burning in the desolation.

sentences.latin: Tum se quieti dedit et quievit verissimo quidem somno; nam meatus animae, qui illi propter amplitudinem corporis gravior et sonantior erat, ab eis qui limini obversabantur audiebatur.
sentences.english: Then he gave himself to rest and rested in a most genuine sleep; for the passage of his breath, which was heavier and more sonorous in him because of his bulk, was heard by those who were near the threshold.

sentences.latin: Sed area ex qua diaeta adibatur ita iam cinere mixtisque pumicibus oppleta surrexerat, ut si longior in cubiculo mora, exitus negaretur.
sentences.english: But the courtyard from which the room was entered had now risen so high, filled with ash mixed with pumice, that if the delay in the bedroom were longer, exit would be denied.

sentences.latin: Excitatus procedit, seque Pomponiano ceterisque qui pervigilaverant reddit.
sentences.english: Awakened, he comes out and rejoins Pomponianus and the others who had stayed up all night.

sentences.latin: In commune consultant, intra tecta subsistant an in aperto vagentur.
sentences.english: They consult together, whether to remain inside the buildings or wander in the open.

sentences.latin: Nam crebris vastisque tremoribus tecta nutabant, et quasi emota sedibus suis nunc huc nunc illuc abire aut referri videbantur.
sentences.english: For the buildings were swaying with frequent and vast tremors, and seemed, as if torn from their foundations, to be moving now here, now there, or being carried back.

sentences.latin: Sub dio rursus quamquam levium exesorumque pumicum casus metuebatur, quod tamen periculorum collatio elegit; et apud illum quidem ratio rationem, apud alios timorem timor vicit.
sentences.english: Under the open sky, on the other hand, the fall of light and porous pumice stones was feared, but a comparison of the dangers settled on this; with him indeed reason overcame reason, with the others fear overcame fear.

sentences.latin: Cervicalia capitibus imposita linteis constringunt; id munimentum adversus incidentia fuit.
sentences.english: They tie pillows on their heads with cloths; this was a defense against the falling debris.

sentences.latin: Iam dies alibi, illic nox omnibus noctibus nigrior densiorque; quam tamen faces multae variaque lumina solabantur.
sentences.english: Day was now elsewhere, there a night blacker and denser than any night; this, however, many torches and various lights relieved.

sentences.latin: Placuit egredi in litus, et ex proximo aspicere, ecquid iam mare admitteret; quod adhuc vastum et adversum permanebat.
sentences.english: It was decided to go out to the shore and to see from close up whether the sea would yet allow anything; it still remained vast and contrary.

sentences.latin: Ibi super abiectum linteum recubans semel atque iterum frigidam aquam poposcit hausitque.
sentences.english: There, lying down on a thrown-down cloth, he asked for cold water once and again and drank it.

sentences.latin: Deinde flammae flammarumque praenuntius odor sulpuris alios in fugam vertunt, excitant illum.
sentences.english: Then flames, and the smell of sulfur announcing flames, turn the others to flight and rouse him.

sentences.latin: Innitens servulis duobus assurrexit et statim concidit, ut ego colligo, crassiore caligine spiritu obstructo, clausoque stomacho qui illi natura invalidus et angustus et frequenter aestuans erat.
sentences.english: Leaning on two slaves, he stood up and immediately collapsed, as I gather, his breathing being obstructed by the thicker fumes and his throat being closed, which by nature was weak and narrow and frequently inflamed.

sentences.latin: Ubi dies redditus (is ab eo quem novissime viderat tertius), corpus inventum integrum illaesum opertumque ut fuerat indutus: habitus corporis quiescenti quam defuncto similior.
sentences.english: When daylight returned (the third from the day he had last seen), his body was found whole, unharmed, and clothed as he had been when dressed: the appearance of the body more like one resting than one dead.

sentences.latin: Interim Miseni ego et mater — sed nihil ad historiam, nec tu aliud quam de exitu eius scire voluisti.
sentences.english: Meanwhile at Misenum I and my mother — but nothing to do with history, nor did you wish to know anything other than about his death.

sentences.latin: Finem ergo faciam.
sentences.english: Therefore I will make an end.

sentences.latin: Unum adiciam, omnia me quibus interfueram quaeque statim, cum maxime vera memorantur, audieram, persecutum.
sentences.english: I will add one thing, that I have followed up on everything I was present for and everything I had heard immediately afterwards, when the truest things are remembered.

sentences.latin: Tu potissima excerpes; aliud est enim epistulam aliud historiam, aliud amico aliud omnibus scribere.
sentences.english: You will pick out the most important parts; for it is one thing to write a letter, another to write history, one thing to write to a friend, another to write to everyone.

sentences.latin: Vale.
sentences.english: Farewell.
